questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded Between a Curve and the Y-Axis by First Rewriting the Function
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059137/assets/9e19c1cd8bca76f1eec39acfa1b09c0f08b67faea5ddce8325e093923d21d394.png)

Find the area bounded between the curve $y=\sqrt[3]{x+1},$ the $y$-axis and the lines $y=0$ and $y=1,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{x+1} \\ {y}^{3} & =x+1 \\ x & ={y}^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{1}-y{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{4}-0)-(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-1 \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So the area that we want is $|-\frac{3}{4}|=\frac{3}{4}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Magnitude of a Vector Given the Coordinates of its Endpoints
questions.problem: Let $A(2,7,0)$ and $B(2,5,4).$ Find a unit vector that is parallel to $\overset{\to }{AB}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned} & \overset{\to }{OA}=a=2i+7j, \\  & \overset{\to }{OB}=b=2i+5j+4k.\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing $\overset{\to }{AB}$ as the difference of position vectors, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{\to }{AB} & =\overset{\to }{OB}-\overset{\to }{OA} \\  & =b-a \\  & =2i+5j+4k-(2i+7j) \\  & =-2j+4k \\  & =⟨0,-2,4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, remember that to find a unit vector that is parallel to a given vector, we need to divide the given vector by its length:

$$
u=\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{|\,\overset{\to }{AB}\,|}
$$

Using the formula for the magnitude of a vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}|\,\overset{\to }{AB}\,| & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+4+16} \\  & =\sqrt{20} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we divide $\overset{\to }{AB}$ by its length and get the following unit vector:

$$
\begin{aligned}u & =\frac{\overset{\to }{AB}}{|\,\overset{\to }{AB}\,|} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\overset{\to }{AB} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{5}}\cdot ⟨0,-2,4⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}},\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Representing Solutions of Compound Inequalities on Number Lines
questions.problem: Which of the following number lines gives the solution to $-9<6-5x<1?$
questions.worked_solution:
We isolate $x$ by applying the addition and multiplication principles, as usual. 

First, we apply the addition principle:

$$
\begin{aligned}-9 & <6-5x<1 \\ -9-6 & <6-5x-6<1-6 \\ -15 & <-5x<-5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we divide by $-5.$ Note that since we are dividing by a negative number, we need to flip the inequality signs. 

$$
\begin{aligned}-15 & <-5x<-5 \\ \frac{-15}{-5} & >\frac{-5x}{-5}>\frac{-5}{-5} \\ 3 & >x>1\end{aligned}
$$

The solution can be written as $3>x>1$, but this is somewhat difficult to read because the larger number is on the left rather than the right. So, we will rewrite the solution by reversing the order of the numbers: 

$$
1<x<3
$$

We can represent this solution using a number line, as follows.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Components of a Vector With Respect to a Given Orthonormal Basis
questions.problem: Given the **orthonormal** basis $B={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]}$ of ${R}^{2},$ find $[x]_{B}$ if $x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $B$ as ${q}_{1},\,{q}_{2}.$ 

Since $B$ is an orthonormal basis, we have that $[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]$, where ${x}_{i}=x\cdot {q}_{i}.$ Computing the components of $x,$ we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ {x}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{4}{\sqrt{2}}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}}=\frac{6}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
[x]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{6}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with a Repeated Root
questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+15x{y}^{′}+49y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y={c}_{1}{x}^{-7}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-7}\operatorname{ln}⁡x,
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+15x{y}^{′}+49y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1,\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- First, we apply the condition $y(1)=1.$ Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

- Then, we apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=1.$ Differentiating $y,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =-7{c}_{1}{x}^{-8}+{c}_{2}{x}^{-8}-7{c}_{2}{x}^{-8}\operatorname{ln}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ and ${c}_{1}=1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =-7(1)+{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & ={x}^{-7}+8{x}^{-7}\operatorname{ln}⁡x \\  & =\frac{1+8\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{x}^{7}}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying Row Operations To a Coefficients Matrix
questions.problem:
Consider the matrix $B,$ given by

$$
B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ -4 & 12 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

What matrix results from carrying out the following row operations on $B?$

$$
\begin{aligned}{R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's list the required operations:

- The operation ${R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1}$ means that we need to add $4$ times the first row to the second row.

- The operation ${R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}$ means that we need to add $1$ times the first row to the third row.

Applying the operations, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}B & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ -4 & 12 & 3 \\ -1 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}]\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4\cdot {R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ -4+(4)(1) & 12+(4)(3) & 3+(4)(6) \\ -1 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 24 & 27 \\ -1 & 2 & 4\end{aligned}]\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 24 & 27 \\ -1+1 & 2+3 & 4+6\end{aligned}] \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 0 & 24 & 27 \\ 0 & 5 & 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Roots of a Transformed Radical Function With an Even Index
questions.problem: Find the root of $f(x)=-3\sqrt[6]{2x-5}-3.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the root of $f(x),$  we must solve $f(x)=0:$

$$
-3\sqrt[6]{2x-5}-3=0
$$

We solve this equation by making $x$ the subject, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-3\sqrt[6]{2x-5}-3 & =0 \\ -3\sqrt[6]{2x-5} & =3 \\ \sqrt[6]{2x-5} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

This equation does not have any solutions since its left-hand side is always nonnegative, while the right-hand side is negative.

Therefore, $f(x)$ has no root.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity of a Particle Whose Acceleration Is Given By a Polynomial
questions.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=2t+{t}^{2}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=\frac{8}{3}\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=1\,\text{s}$, calculate the velocity of the particle at the moment $t=2\,\text{s}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\text{d}t \\  & =\int (2t+{t}^{2})\text{d}t \\  & ={t}^{2}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(1)=\frac{8}{3}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{3} & =(1)^{2}+\frac{(1)^{3}}{3}+C \\ \frac{8}{3} & =1+\frac{1}{3}+C \\ C & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=\frac{4}{3}+{t}^{2}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}.$

We evaluate the velocity at time $t=2\,\text{s}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(2) & =\frac{4}{3}+(2)^{2}+\frac{(2)^{3}}{3} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}+4+\frac{8}{3} \\  & =8\,\text{m/s}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a 2x2 System of Equations Using an Inverse Matrix With Reorganization
questions.problem:
Which of the following represents the solution to the system of linear equations given below?

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}3y=-x \\ 2y=1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we reorganize the equations so that they are in the right order, to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}x+3y=0 \\ 2y=1.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can represent this system of equations in the form $Ax=b:$

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the solution, we need to calculate the inverse of the coefficient matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{1\cdot 2-0\cdot 3}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the solution to this system as:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & ={A}^{-1}b \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Radius and Interval of Convergence of a Power Series
questions.problem:
Find the radius of convergence $R$ and interval of convergence $I$ for the series

$$
{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x+5)^{n}}{n(n+1)}\,.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To apply the ratio test, we define ${a}_{n}=\frac{(x+5)^{n}}{n(n+1)}.$ Then, we calculate the ratio of two successive terms and take the limit as $n\to \infty :$

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{{a}_{n+1}}{{a}_{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{(x+5)^{n+1}}{(n+1)(n+2)}\cdot \frac{n(n+1)}{(x+5)^{n}}| \\  & ={lim}_{n\to \infty }|\frac{n(x+5)}{n+2}| \\  & =|x+5|{lim}_{n\to \infty }\frac{n}{n+2} \\  & =|x+5|{lim}_{n\to \infty }(\frac{1}{(1+\frac{2}{n})}) \\  & =|x+5|\cdot 1 \\  & =|x+5|\end{aligned}
$$

The series converges if $L<1.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}|x+5| & <1 \\ -1<x+5 & <1 \\ -6<x & <-4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the radius of convergence is $R=1,$ and the series converges for any $x$ that lies in the open interval $(-6,-4).$

The ratio test gives no conclusion about the convergence of the series when $L=1.$ So, when $|x+5|=1,$ we do not know if the series converges. This means that the endpoints $x=-6$ and $x=-4$ need to be investigated separately using another test for convergence.

- When $x=-6$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x+5)^{n}}{n(n+1)} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-6+5)^{n}}{n(n+1)} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-1)^{n}}{{n}^{2}+n}\end{aligned}
$$

which is convergent by the alternating series test.

- When $x=-4$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(x+5)^{n}}{n(n+1)} & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{(-4+5)^{n}}{n(n+1)} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{{1}^{n}}{{n}^{2}+n} \\  & ={\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}+n}\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the above series with  ${\sum }_{n=1}^{\infty }\frac{1}{{n}^{2}},$
we see that the series is convergent by the comparison test.

So the interval of convergence is $I=[-6,-4].$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Factors Giving an Exact ODE
questions.problem:
Consider the following differential equation:

$$
P(x,y)\text{d}x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)\text{d}y=0
$$

Given that the differential equation is exact, which of the following functions could be $P(x,y)?$

- $y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-y$
- $xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)$
- $y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)$
questions.worked_solution:
A differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\text{d}y=0
$$

is exact if it passes the exactness test, i.e.,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}.
$$

In our case, we're given $Q(x,y)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy).$ 

First, let's differentiate $Q(x,y)$ with respect to $x$:

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)
$$

Now, let's apply $\frac{∂}{∂y}$ to each of the given options:

- First, we check $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-y.$ This gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)-1\ne \frac{∂Q}{∂x}\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-y$ does *not* give an exact equation.

- Next, we check $P(x,y)=xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))=x\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-{x}^{2}y\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)\ne \frac{∂Q}{∂x}\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x,y)=xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)$ does *not* give an exact equation.

- Finally, we check $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)-xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(xy)$  gives an exact equation.

Hence, the correct answer is ''III only''.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Inverse of a 3x3 Matrix Using the Matrix of Cofactors
questions.problem:
Find the inverse of the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]$
given that $det(A)=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's follow the standard five-step procedure.

**Step 1:** We are given the determinant of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A)=4\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2:** Form the matrix of the minors of $A.$
To make this matrix, we replace each entry of $A$ by its minor.

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\ |\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}| & |\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 3 \\ -2 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3:** Create the matrix of cofactors by changing the sign of some of the entries of $M$ according to the rule of alternating signs.

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & -3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 4:** Write down the transpose of the matrix of cofactors.

$$
{C}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 5:** Use the formula for the inverse of a $3\times 3$ matrix.

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{det(A)}{C}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying First-Order Linear ODEs
questions.problem: Which of the following is a first-order linear ordinary differential equation?
questions.worked_solution:
To determine which of the following differential equations is a first-order linear ordinary differential equation, we attempt to write each option in the standard form.

A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Let's attempt to write $\frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-x{e}^{2x}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{y}$ in the standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{y}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-x{e}^{2x} & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-x{e}^{2x}y & =y\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{y} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-x{e}^{2x}y & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is in standard form with  $P(x)=-x{e}^{2x}$ and $Q(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x.$ Since the equation is written in standard form, we conclude that it is a first-order linear ODE.

All of the other equations cannot be written in the standard form, and therefore they are not first-order linear ODEs.

questions.knowledge_point: Applications of Accumulation Functions
questions.problem: The bacteria culture in a lab increases at a rate of ${e}^{2t}$ per hour. If, after $2$ hours, there are $2\,000$ bacteria in the population, approximately how many bacteria are in the population after $6$ hours?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $s(t)={e}^{2t}$ be the rate at which the number of bacteria is changing and let $S(T)$ be the total number of bacteria and in the population after $T$ hours.

Using our formula for the accumulation of change, we have

$$
S(T)=S(2)+{\int }_{2}^{T}s(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

Substituting the known information and carrying out the necessary integration gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(T) & =S(2)+{\int }_{2}^{T}s(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\,000+{\int }_{2}^{T}{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\,000+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}{|}_{2}^{T} \\  & =2\,000+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2T}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2\cdot 2} \\  & =2\,000+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2T}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to find the number of bacteria in the culture after $T=6$ hours, we substitute in the above:

$$
S(6)=2\,000+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2\cdot 6}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4}=2\,000+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{12}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{4}≈83\,350.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Rate of Change of a Leg Using the Pythagorean Theorem
questions.problem: A hot air balloon that is launched vertically is observed by a child located on the ground $4\,\text{km}$ from the launch site. What is the vertical speed of the balloon at the instant when its distance from the child is $5\,\text{km}$ and this distance is increasing at a rate of $12\,\text{km/h}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by drawing a diagram of the problem.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14066033/assets/40957ce27304474263d1d231a3a0df93193ac0461d8a7444cde3b12047d1a214.png)

In the diagram,

- $x$ is the distance between the child and the launch site,

- $y$ is the distance between the launch site and the balloon,

- $z$ is the distance between the child and the balloon.

As shown in the diagram, $x,$ $y,$ and $z$ form a right triangle with $z$ as the hypotenuse. We wish to find the rate of change of $y,$ which is $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}.$ 

We know that $z=5\,\text{km}$ and $x=4\,\text{km}.$ We can find $y$ using the Pythagorean Theorem, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2} & ={z}^{2} \\ {4}^{2}+{y}^{2} & ={5}^{2} \\ {y}^{2} & =9 \\ y & =3\,\text{km}\end{aligned}
$$

We also know that:

- $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}=12\,\text{km}/\text{h},$

- the distance between the child and the launch site ($x$) remains the same, so $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=0.$

Finally, we differentiate both sides of ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}={z}^{2}$ with respect to $t$ and then substitute in the known values, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({z}^{2}) \\ 2x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+2y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2z\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} \\ 2(4)(0)+2(3)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =2(5)(12) \\ 6\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =120 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{120}{6} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =20\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vertical speed of the hot air balloon is $20\,\text{km}/\text{h}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Center and Radius of a Circle by Completing the Square with Fractions
questions.problem:
Find the radius and center of the circle whose equation is
${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+7x=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the center and radius of the circle, we need to group $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares.

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+7x & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}+7x)+{y}^{2} & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{7}{2}x+{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2})+{y}^{2} & ={(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can factor the perfect square and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{(x+\frac{7}{2})}^{2}+{y}^{2} & ={(\frac{7}{2})}^{2} \\ {(x-(-\frac{7}{2}))}^{2}+(y-0)^{2} & ={(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the circle is centered at $(-\frac{7}{2},0)$ and its radius is $\frac{7}{2}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Indefinite Integral of a Rational Function Using Partial Fractions
questions.problem:
Given that

$$
\int \frac{7}{(x-1)(x+6)}\,\text{d}x=a\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|+b\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+6|+C,
$$

find the value of $a+b.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{(x-1)(x+6)} & =\frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x+6},\end{aligned}
$$

which gives

$$
7=A(x+6)+B(x-1).
$$

Plugging in $x=-6,$ we can eliminate $A$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}7 & =A(-6+6)+B(-6-1) \\ 7 & =-7B \\ B & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand, plugging in $x=1,$ we can eliminate $B$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}7 & =A(1+6)+B(1-1) \\ 7 & =7A \\ A & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{7}{(x-1)(x+6)} & =\frac{1}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x+6}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7}{(x-1)(x+6)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x-1}-\frac{1}{x+6})\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x-1}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{1}{x+6}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-1|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+6|+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $a=1,b=-1,$ and $a+b=1-1=0.$

questions.knowledge_point: Optimizing the Area of a Rectangle
questions.problem: A gardener wants to fence a rectangular flowerbed with $15$ meters of fencing. To two decimal places, what is the largest area that he can make with the fencing?
questions.worked_solution:
**Step 1**: Let us call $x$ and $y$ the dimensions of the rectangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067869/assets/bebb7c4ca5e38d75136146f6e4547b0e72d529ce24453a3d0212bca1ffbfe4c0.png)

**Step 2**: We need to find the values of $x$ and $y$ such as the area

$$
A=xy
$$

is the greatest possible value.

**Step 3**: This is subject to the constraint that the perimeter is $15.$ This gives the equation

$$
2x+2y=15.
$$

**Step 4**: We make one of the variables the subject in the constraint equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+2y & =15 \\ y & =\frac{15}{2}-x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $y=\frac{15}{2}-x$ in the expression $A=xy$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =x(\frac{15}{2}-x) \\ A & =\frac{15}{2}x-{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**: We solve the equation ${A}^{′}(x)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{A}^{′}(x)=\frac{15}{2}-2x,
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ \frac{15}{2}-2x & =0 \\ 2x & =\frac{15}{2} \\ x & =\frac{15}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 6**: We confirm that $x=\frac{15}{4}$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{A}^{″}(x)=-2\,⟹\,{A}^{″}(\frac{15}{4})=-2<0.
$$

Since ${A}^{″}(\frac{15}{4})$ is negative, we conclude that $x=\frac{15}{4}$ is indeed a maximum of $A(x).$

Finally, when $x=\frac{15}{4}$, we have 

$$
y=\frac{15}{2}-\frac{15}{4}=\frac{15}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the dimensions of the rectangle with the largest area are $x=\frac{15}{4}$ and $y=\frac{15}{4},$ and we conclude that

$$
A=xy=\frac{15}{4}\cdot \frac{15}{4}≈14.06
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Vector Field Corresponding to a Given Potential Function
questions.problem: For which of the following vector fields is $f(x,y)=y{e}^{xy}$ a potential function?
questions.worked_solution:
A vector field $F$ is conservative if it is the gradient of a scalar function $f.$ That is, there exists a function $f$ such that $F=∇f.$ The function $f$ is called a potential function for $F.$

To compute the vector field associated with a potential function $f,$ we compute its gradient:

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{e}^{xy})\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy})\,j \\  & ={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}\,i+(xy+1){e}^{xy}\,j \\  & =F\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field that has $f$ as a potential function is

$$
F={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}\,i+(xy+1){e}^{xy}\,j.
$$

questions.problem:
A ball is dropped vertically downward from a height of $44.1\,\text{m}.$ How long does it take for the ball to hit the ground?

*Hint: The acceleration due to gravity is $9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$*

To solve this problem, we use the formula

$$
s=ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2},
$$

where $s$ is the displacement, measured from the starting position in the direction of the initial motion, $u$ is the initial velocity, $t$ is the time since the beginning of the motion, and $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity.

Let's summarize the information we have:

- The initial velocity of the ball is $u=0\,\text{m/s}.$

- The ball covers the distance of $s=44.1\,\text{m}.$

- The acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

Substituting these values into the formula and solving for $t,$ we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =ut+\frac{1}{2}g{t}^{2} \\ 44.1 & =(0)t+\frac{1}{2}(9.8){t}^{2} \\ 44.1 & =4.9{t}^{2} \\ {t}^{2} & =\frac{44.1}{4.9} \\ {t}^{2} & =9 \\ t & =\pm 3\end{aligned}
$$

We disregard the negative solution. Therefore, the ball hits the ground after $t=3$ seconds.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding and Classifying All Critical Points Using the Second Partial Derivatives Test
questions.problem:
Find and categorize all the local extrema of the function 
$f(x,y)$ 
given that

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-y & 8{y}^{2}-x\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The local extrema of $f$ occur at its critical points. A point $a$ in the domain of $f$ is a critical point of $f$ if ${f}^{′}(a)={0}^{T}$ (for stationary points) or ${f}^{′}(a)$ doesn't exist.

The second partial derivative test states that if $a\in {R}^{2}$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y)$ with Hessian determinant $H(a),$ we have the following:

- If $H(a)>0,$ then:

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a local maximum at $a$

- if $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(a)>0,$ then $f$ has a local minimum at $a$

- If $H(a)<0,$ then $f$ has a saddle point at $a$

- If $H(a)=0,$ then the second partial derivatives test is inconclusive.

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-y & 8{y}^{2}-x\end{aligned}],$ we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}={x}^{2}-y,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=8{y}^{2}-x.
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting ${f}^{′}(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-y=0 \\ 8{y}^{2}-x=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{2}-y=0\,⟹\,y={x}^{2}.
$$

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}8{({x}^{2})}^{2}-x & =0 \\ 8{x}^{4}-x & =0 \\ x(8{x}^{3}-1) & =0 \\ x & =0,\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Back-substituting these values into $y={x}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
x=0\,\,\,\,⟹\,y={0}^{2}=0,\,\,x=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,y={(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}=\frac{1}{4}.
$$

Hence, $(0,0)$ and $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4})$ are stationary points of $f(x,y).$

To classify these stationary points, we use the second partial derivative test.

First, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-y)=2x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{y}^{2}-x)=-1 \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-y)=-1\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(8{y}^{2}-x)=16y\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2x & -1 \\ -1 & 16y\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the second derivative at each of the stationary points and use it to categorize them:

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(0,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(0,0)=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(0,0),$ we get

$$
H(0,0)=det({f}^{″}(0,0))={0}^{2}-(-1)^{2}=-1<0,
$$

Therefore, $f(0,0)$ is a saddle point.

- Evaluating the second derivative at $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4})=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}),$ we get

$$
H(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4})=det({f}^{″}(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}))=1\cdot 4-(-1)^{2}=3>0
$$

Finally, since $H(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4})>0$ and $\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}}(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4})={h}_{11}=1>0.$ Therefore, we have a local minimum at $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}).$

In conclusion, $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(0,0)$ and a local minimum at $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}).$

$$
\begin{aligned}f′(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{ln}⁡x-{y}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x} & \operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The first derivative exists for any $(x,y)$ in the domain of the function, so we only need to find the stationary points. Setting $f′(x,y)={0}^{T},$ we obtain the following system:

$$
{\begin{aligned}\frac{y}{x}=0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation for $y,$ we get

$$
\frac{y}{x}=0\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

Then, substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2(0)=\operatorname{ln}⁡x=0\,⟹\,x=1.
$$

Hence, $(1,0)$ is a stationary point of $f(x,y).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{y}{x})=-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y)=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{y}{x})=\frac{1}{x}\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x-2y)=-2\end{aligned}

So, the second derivative  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{1}{x} & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the second derivative at $(1,0),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(1,0)=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Computing the determinant $H(1,0),$ we get

$$
H(1,0)=det({f}^{″}(1,0))=0\cdot (-2)-{1}^{2}=-1<0.
$$

Therefore, applying the second partial derivative test, we have that $f(x,y)$ has a saddle point at $(1,0).$

questions.problem: Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function $r(u,v)=⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,{v}^{2},\,4v\operatorname{cos}⁡u⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface with parametrization $r(u,v),$ the fundamental vector product is defined as ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}.$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(\operatorname{sin}⁡u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(4v\operatorname{cos}⁡u)⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡u,\,0,\,-4v\operatorname{sin}⁡u⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(\operatorname{sin}⁡u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(4v\operatorname{cos}⁡u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2v,\,4\operatorname{cos}⁡u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡u & 0 & -4v\operatorname{sin}⁡u \\ 0 & 2v & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡u\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & -4v\operatorname{sin}⁡u \\ 2v & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡u\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u & -4v\operatorname{sin}⁡u \\ 0 & 4\operatorname{cos}⁡u\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡u & 0 \\ 0 & 2v\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨8{v}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,-4{cos}^{2}⁡u,\,2v\operatorname{cos}⁡u⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Curl of a Vector Field
questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\,i+y{z}^{2}\,j+(x-z)\,k.$ Evaluate $∇\times F$ at the point  $(2,-1,3).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the curl of $F$ is the vector field given by

$$
curl\,F=∇\times F=|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ P & Q & R\end{aligned}|.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ \frac{∂}{∂x} & \frac{∂}{∂y} & \frac{∂}{∂z} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & y{z}^{2} & (x-z)\end{aligned}| \\  & =[\frac{∂}{∂y}(x-z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(y{z}^{2})]i-[\frac{∂}{∂x}(x-z)-\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))]j+[\frac{∂}{∂x}(y{z}^{2})-\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y))]k \\  & =(0-2yz)i-(1-0)j+(0-\frac{1}{x+y})k \\  & =-2yz\,i-j-\frac{1}{x+y}\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{curl}\,F$ at the point $(2,-1,3),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(\text{curl}\,F)(2,-1,3) & =-2(-1)(3)\,i-j-\frac{1}{2+(-1)}\,k \\  & =6\,i-j-k.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Number of Solutions Given a Table of Values of a Continuous Function
questions.problem:
The function $g(x)$ is continuous over $x\in [2,7].$ Some values of $g(x)$ are given in the table below. 

| $x$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ | $7$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $g(x)$ | $-2$ | $1$ | $-3$ | $1$ | $0$ | $2$ |

What is the smallest possible number of solutions to the equation $g(x)=-1?$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $g$ is a continuous function on $[2,7]$, we can apply the intermediate value theorem (IVT) in any subinterval of $[2,7].$

So, we will go through each subinterval of $[2,7]$ and check if the IVT guarantees a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1.$

- On the subinterval $[2,3],$ we have $g(2)=-2$ and $g(3)=1.$ Since $-1\in [-2,1],$  the IVT *does * guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[3,4],$ we have $g(3)=1$ and $g(4)=-3.$ Since $-1\in [-3,1],$ the IVT *does* guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[4,5],$ we have $g(4)=-3$ and $g(5)=1.$ Since $-1\in [-3,1],$ the IVT *does * guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[5,6],$ we have $g(5)=1$ and $g(6)=0.$ Since $-1\notin [0,1],$ the IVT does *not* guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1$ on this subinterval.

- On the subinterval $[6,7],$ we have $g(6)=0$ and $g(7)=2.$ Since $-1\notin [0,2],$ the IVT does *not* guarantee a solution to the equation $g(x)=-1$ on this subinterval.

The IVT guarantees solutions to $g(x)=-1$ on the subintervals $[2,3],$ $[3,4]$  and $[4,5].$ Therefore, $g(x)=-1$ has at least three solutions on $[2,7].$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Curl of a Vector Field Using the Product Rule
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨-1,0,x{y}^{3}⟩$ and the scalar field $f(x,y,z)=yz.$ Given that

$$
∇\times F=⟨3x{y}^{2},-{y}^{3},0⟩,\,∇f=⟨0,z,y⟩,
$$

calculate $∇\times (f\,F)$ at the point $(0,-1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
We shall use the following identity:

$$
∇\times (f\,F)=f∇\times F+∇f\times F
$$

First, we compute $∇f\times F.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f\times F & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & z & y \\ -1 & 0 & x{y}^{3}\end{aligned}| \\  & =[z(x{y}^{3})-y(0)]i-[0(x{y}^{3})-y(-1)]j+[0(0)-z(-1)]k \\  & =xz{y}^{3}\,i-y\,j+z\,k \\  & =⟨xz{y}^{3},-y,z⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F) & =f∇\times F+∇f\times F \\  & =yz⟨3x{y}^{2},-{y}^{3},0⟩+⟨xz{y}^{3},-y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨3xz{y}^{3},-z{y}^{4},0⟩+⟨xz{y}^{3},-y,z⟩ \\  & =⟨4xz{y}^{3},-z{y}^{4}-y,z⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\times (f\,F)(0,-1,2) & =⟨4(0)(2)(-1)^{3},-2(-1)^{4}-(-1),2⟩ \\  & =⟨0,-1,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Surface of Revolution
questions.problem: Use a fundamental vector product to determine which of the following integrals gives the surface area generated when the curve $x=1+{y}^{2}$ is rotated by $2\pi $ radians about the $y$-axis for $y\in [-1,1].$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $x=1+{y}^{2}\ge 0$ for all $y\in [-1,1].$ The parametrization of our surface of revolution is

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨f(y)\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,y,\,f(y)\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩,\,(y,\theta )\in D\end{aligned}
$$

where $f(y)=1+{y}^{2},$ and

$$
D={(y,\theta )\,:\,-1\le y\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂y},\,\frac{∂y}{∂y}\,\frac{∂z}{∂y}⟩=⟨{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,1,\,{f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\ {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂y}{∂\theta },\,\frac{∂z}{∂\theta }⟩=⟨-f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,\,0,\,f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ {f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}1 & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ 0 & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & {f}^{′}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  & 1 \\ -f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  & 0\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -f{f}^{′}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ,\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩ \\  & =⟨f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\,-f{f}^{′},\,f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ⟩\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖ & =\sqrt{(f\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(-f{f}^{′})^{2}+(f\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{f}^{2}+{f}^{2}({f}^{′})^{2}} \\  & =f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{y}^{′}\times {r}_{\theta }^{′}‖\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={∬}_{D}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta \,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $f=1+{y}^{2},$ we obtain ${f}^{′}=2y.$ So, finally, we conclude that our expression for the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}f\sqrt{1+({f}^{′})^{2}}\,\text{d}y & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}(1+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1+(2y)^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{-1}^{1}(1+{y}^{2})\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

The eigenvectors of $A$ are the non-zero vectors $v$ such that $Av=\lambda v.$ We have

$$
[\begin{aligned}16 \\ -8\end{aligned}]=\lambda [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4\end{aligned}].
$$

This leads to the following system of equations for $\lambda :$

$$
{\begin{aligned}16=2\lambda  \\ -8=-4\lambda \end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Inhibited Decay Model
questions.problem:
Simon measures the temperature of the tea in his cup, and the thermometer displays a reading of ${60}^{∘}C.$ After $10$ minutes, Simon repeats the measurement and the thermometer displays a reading of  ${52}^{∘}C.$ To the nearest minute, how long does it take for the tea to decrease its temperature to ${40}^{∘}C$ if the temperature in the room is ${28}^{∘}C?$ 

*Hint: You may assume that the temperature $T(t)$ of the tea in Simon's cup decreases at a rate that obeys Newton's law of cooling, where $T$ is measured in degrees Celsius and $t>0$ is the time, in minutes, since the first measurement.*
questions.worked_solution:
Newton's law of cooling states that the rate at which the temperature $T(t)$ of a body changes is proportional to the difference between its temperature and its surroundings. Therefore, we have the inhibited decay equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-{T}_{S}),
$$

where ${T}_{S}$ is the temperature of the surroundings, and $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality.

In our case, ${T}_{S}={28}^{∘}\text{C},$ and we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}T}{\text{d}t}=-k(T-28).
$$

First, we integrate our differential equation by separating the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\,dt \\ \int \frac{dT}{T-28} & =-k\int dt \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|T-28| & =-kt+C\end{aligned}
$$

Since this is the solution to an inhibited decay equation, we have $T-28>0$ for all $t>0.$
Next, we solve for $T(t),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T-28 & ={e}^{-kt+C} \\ T-28 & ={e}^{C}{e}^{-kt} \\ T-28 & =K{e}^{-kt} \\ T & =28+K{e}^{-kt}\end{aligned}
$$

Note that $K={e}^{C}$ is a constant of integration. 

We're told that the initial temperature reading was ${60}^{∘}C.$ So, we apply the initial condition $T(0)=60,$ and solve for $K:$

$$
\begin{aligned}60 & =28+K{e}^{0} \\ 60 & =28+K \\ K & =32\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have the following expression for $T(t):$

$$
T(t)=28+32{e}^{-kt}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Eigenvector Corresponding to an Eigenvalue
questions.problem: Find an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}22 & -40 \\ -5 & 5\end{aligned}]$ that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-3.$ So, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}22 & -40 \\ -5 & 5\end{aligned}]-(-3)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}25 & -40 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}25{x}_{1}-40{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}25 & -40 \\ -5 & 8\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{5}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}25 & -40 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. 

From the first equation, we obtain 

$$
25{x}_{1}-40{x}_{2}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=\frac{8}{5}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{8}{5}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Finally, setting ${x}_{2}=5,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{4}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\,.\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Reducing an Inhomogeneous ODE to First-Order System
questions.problem:
The third-order differential equation 

$$
{y}^{‴}-\sqrt{t}\,{y}^{″}-y={t}^{2}
$$

can be written as a system of first-order differential equations, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

where ${x}_{1}(t)=y(t),$ ${x}_{2}(t)={y}^{′}(t)$ and ${x}_{3}(t)={y}^{″}(t).$ Find the function $f(t).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(t) & =y \\ {x}_{2}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{3}(t) & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{″} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}(t) & ={y}^{‴}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={y}^{‴}.\end{aligned}
$$

At this point, we're almost done. We just need to write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1},$ ${x}_{2},$ and ${x}_{3}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{‴}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{‴}=\sqrt{t}\,{y}^{″}+y+{t}^{2}.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{‴}=\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}+{x}_{1}+{t}^{2}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3}, \\ {x}_{3}^{′}={x}_{1}+\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}+{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
f(t)={x}_{1}+\sqrt{t}\,{x}_{3}+{t}^{2}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing a Homogeneous ODE as a Matrix Differential Equation
questions.problem:
The second-order differential equation ${y}^{″}-2{y}^{′}+y=0$
can be expressed as the matrix equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ where 

$$
x(t)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}],\,y(t)={x}_{1}(t),\,{y}^{′}(t)={x}_{2}(t).
$$

Find the matrix $A.$
questions.worked_solution:
We first need to express the given differential equation as a system of first-order differential equations. Then, we write the system as a matrix equation.

We start by making the following change of variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =y \\ {x}_{2} & ={y}^{′}\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiating the above equations with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} & ={y}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′} & ={y}^{″}\end{aligned}
$$

which we can rewrite as 

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2}, \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={y}^{″}.\end{aligned}
$$

We must now write the right-hand side of the last equation in terms of ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}.$

Solving our original differential equation for the highest-order derivative $({y}^{″}),$ we obtain

$$
{y}^{″}=2{y}^{′}-y.
$$

Then, we substitute our new variables into the right-hand side of the above equation. This gives

$$
{y}^{″}=2{x}_{2}-{x}_{1}.
$$

Notice that we do not include any derivative terms on the right-hand side. 

Therefore, our complete system of equations is as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}=-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can represent this system as the matrix differential equation ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)$ as follows:

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Hence, $A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(2+3{e}^{-x})\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=3\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14041958/assets/ec4af1357e75dcee6d7d5412467c2ee2ea9e54fa38fb6e83817b0ae909c529aa.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2+3{e}^{-x})\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2+3{e}^{-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2+3{e}^{-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int (2+3{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2x-3{e}^{-x}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =2(0)-3{e}^{-0}+C \\ 2 & =-3+C \\ C & =2+3 \\ C & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2x-3{e}^{-x}+5 \\ {v}^{2} & =4x-6{e}^{-x}+10 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{4x-6{e}^{-x}+10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{4x-6{e}^{-x}+10}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=3$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{4(3)-6{e}^{-3}+10} \\ v & =\sqrt{22-6{e}^{-3}} \\ v & ≈4.7\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Displacement of a Particle as a Function of Time
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $2{e}^{-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=2\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14064798/assets/ad437638f22672a10a183f1521929637f8d43725f37a9736c569516232e7c468.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $2{e}^{-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2{e}^{-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-2{e}^{-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -2{e}^{-x}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =2{e}^{0}+K \\ K & =2-2 \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x} \\ {v}^{2} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ v & =\pm 2{e}^{-x/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=2{e}^{-x/2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2{e}^{-x/2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2{e}^{-x/2} \\ {e}^{x/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2 \\ \int {e}^{x/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{x/2}\text{d}x & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ 2{e}^{x/2} & =2t+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{x/2} & =t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
{e}^{x/2}=t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x/2} & =t+1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x/2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1) \\ \frac{x}{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1) \\ x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 2x2 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
questions.problem:
Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 5 \\ -10 & -9\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix. 

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}6-\lambda  & 5 \\ -10 & -9-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (6-\lambda )(-9-\lambda )-(5)(-10) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+3\lambda -4 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)(\lambda +4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-4.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{1}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-4)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
Find the intersection point of the line $l$ and the plane $Π$ with equations

$$
l:\frac{x-3}{5}=\frac{y-1}{2}=\frac{z+4}{3},\,Π:r\cdot ⟨-3,2,-1⟩=39.
$$

From the equation of the line $l$, we know that it passes through the point $A(3,1,-4)$ and it is parallel to the vector $v=⟨5,2,3⟩.$ Therefore, its vector equation is given by

\begin{aligned}r & =⟨3,1,-4⟩+t⟨5,2,3⟩ \\  & =⟨3+5t,1+2t,-4+3t⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).$

Now, substituting $r=⟨3+5t,1+2t,-4+3t⟩$ into the equation of the plane, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}r\cdot ⟨-3,2,-1⟩ & =39 \\ ⟨3+5t,1+2t,-4+3t⟩\cdot ⟨-3,2,-1⟩ & =39 \\ (-3)(3+5t)+2(1+2t)-(-4+3t) & =39 \\ -9-15t+2+4t+4-3t & =39 \\ -14t & =42 \\ t & =-3.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}p & =⟨3+5(-3),1+2(-3),-4+3(-3)⟩ \\  & =⟨-12,-5,-13⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some real number $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}-xy=\frac{\sqrt[3]{y}}{{x}^{5}}
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-x,\,q(x)={x}^{-5},\,n=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{1/3},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-1/3}\frac{dy}{dx}-x{y}^{2/3}=\frac{1}{{x}^{5}}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{2/3}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{3}{y}^{-1/3}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-1/3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\frac{3}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-x\,z=\frac{1}{{x}^{5}}
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{2x}{3}\,z=\frac{2}{3{x}^{5}}.
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=-\frac{2x}{3}.$

$$

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

$$
S=2\pi {\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}y\sqrt{1+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Bernoulli Differential Equation
questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={x}^{3}{y}^{2}+xy.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & ={x}^{3}{y}^{2}+xy \\ {x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-xy & ={x}^{3}{y}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-\frac{y}{x} & =x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-\frac{1}{x},\,q(x)=x,\,n=2.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-\frac{{y}^{-1}}{x}=x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{x}z=x
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z=-x
$$

The above equation is now in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x),
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot (-x) \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =-{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & =-{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,\text{d}x & =-\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ xz & =-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-{x}^{3}}{3x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
{y}^{-1}=\frac{C-{x}^{3}}{3x}\,⇒\,y=\frac{3x}{C-{x}^{3}}\,.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Velocity of a Particle at the Moment When Its Acceleration is Zero
questions.problem:
A particle $P$ is traveling along the $x$-axis with displacement $s(t)$ from a fixed origin $O$ given by

$$
s(t)=2{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}+3t-2,\,t\ge 0.
$$

Find the time at which the acceleration is zero, and find the value of the velocity at this moment.

First, we calculate $v(t)$ by differentiating $s(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2{t}^{3}-9{t}^{2}+3t-2) \\  & =6{t}^{2}-18t+3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we differentiate $v(t)$ to find $a(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{t}^{2}-18t+3) \\  & =12t-18\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we put $a=0$ to find the time when the acceleration is zero:

$$
\begin{aligned}12t-18 & =0 \\ t & =\frac{18}{12} \\ t & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the acceleration is zero when $t=\frac{3}{2}.$ To find the velocity at this moment, we substitute this back into $v(t)$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}v(\frac{3}{2}) & =6{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-18(\frac{3}{2})+3 \\  & =6(\frac{9}{4})-27+3 \\  & =\frac{27}{2}-27+3 \\  & =-\frac{21}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 2x2 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
questions.problem:
Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Every $n\times n$ matrix $A$ can be written in the form

$$
A=PJ{P}^{-1},
$$

where $J$ is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of $A,$ and $P$ is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix $J,$ we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ by solving $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & -1 \\ 2 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(3-\lambda )-(-1)(2) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda +2 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)(\lambda -1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the eigenvalues are ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=2.$ Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix $A$ is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

$$
J={J}_{1}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(2)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 1\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 3 \\ 3 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 3 & 3\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0\end{aligned}

{y}^{‴}=3{y}^{′}-4y.

{y}^{‴}=3{x}_{2}-4{x}_{1}.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}^{′}={x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}^{′}={x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}^{′}=-4{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Fundamental Vector Product of a Parametric Surface
questions.problem: Find the fundamental vector product of the surface generated by the vector-valued function $r(u,v)=⟨u,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,v\operatorname{cos}⁡u⟩.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface with parametrization $r(u,v),$ the fundamental vector product is defined as ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}.$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u\operatorname{sin}⁡v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v\operatorname{cos}⁡u)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,-v\operatorname{sin}⁡u⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u\operatorname{sin}⁡v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v\operatorname{cos}⁡u)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡u⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & \operatorname{sin}⁡v & -v\operatorname{sin}⁡u \\ 0 & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \operatorname{cos}⁡u\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡v & -v\operatorname{sin}⁡u \\ u\operatorname{cos}⁡v & \operatorname{cos}⁡u\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & -v\operatorname{sin}⁡u \\ 0 & \operatorname{cos}⁡u\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & \operatorname{sin}⁡v \\ 0 & u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v+uv\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,-\operatorname{cos}⁡u,\,u\operatorname{cos}⁡v⟩.\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Graph of a Strict Inequality Given in Standard Form
questions.problem: Which of the following shaded areas describes the region bounded by the inequality $5x-10y<-20?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we convert the inequality into slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}5x-10y & <-20 \\ -10y & <-5x-20 \\ 10y & >5x+20 \\ y & >\frac{1}{2}x+2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we proceed as usual. We start by drawing the corresponding straight line $y=\frac{1}{2}x+2.$ Since the inequality involves a 'strictly greater than' sign, the line $y=\frac{1}{2}x+2$ itself is *not* part of the solution. Therefore, we draw a dashed line.

Then, we need to decide whether to shade above or below the line. The inequality $y>\frac{1}{2}x+2$ refers to the $y$-values that are *greater than* those on the line $y=\frac{1}{2}x+2,$ so we shade *above* the line.

questions.problem:
$$
{∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A,\,D={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 2}
$$

The integral above gives the surface area of the parametric surface $r(u,v)=⟨u+v,\,3-v,\,1+4u+5v⟩$ for $0\le u\le 1$ and $0\le v\le 2.$ What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(3-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(1+4u+5v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,4⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u+v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(3-v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(1+4u+5v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,-1,\,5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 4 \\ 1 & -1 & 5\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ -1 & 5\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,-1,\,-1⟩,\end{aligned}
$$

and 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖ & =‖⟨4,\,-1,\,-1⟩‖ \\  & =\sqrt{(4)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16+1+1} \\  & =\sqrt{18} \\  & =3\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface area is

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}‖{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}‖\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\sqrt{2}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Normal Vector to a Parametric Surface Given a Point on the Surface
questions.problem: Compute a normal vector to the parametric surface generated by the vector-valued function $r(u,v)=⟨u,\,{v}^{2},\,{u}^{2}-v⟩$ at the point $(1,1,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, notice that since $(1,1,2)$ lies on the surface, we obtain

$$
{\begin{aligned}u=1 \\ {v}^{2}=1 \\ {u}^{2}-v=2\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}u=1 \\ v=-1.\end{aligned}
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}(u,v) & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}({u}^{2}-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,2u⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′}(u,v) & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({v}^{2}),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}({u}^{2}-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,2v,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate these tangent vectors when $u=1$ and $v=-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}(1,-1) & =⟨1,\,0,\,2(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′}(1,-1) & =⟨0,\,2(-1),\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,-2,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a normal vector to the surface at the point $(1,1,2)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}n & ={r}_{u}^{′}(1,-1)\times {r}_{v}^{′}(1,-1) \\  & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & -2 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨4,\,1,\,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Now consider the line $y=\frac{1}{2}x+1.$ Since the line is solid, the inequality is an "or equal to" inequality. Also, since the shaded region lies *below* the line, the inequality is a "less than" inequality. So the corresponding inequality is

$$
y\le \frac{1}{2}x+1.
$$

Therefore, the system of inequalities that defines the shaded region is

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying an Elementary 3x3 Matrix
questions.problem:
Which of the following are elementary matrices?

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Remember that an elementary matrix is obtained by performing exactly one elementary row operation on the identity matrix $I.$

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

- The matrix $A$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{1}↔{R}_{3},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1}↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =A\end{aligned}
$$

- The matrix $B$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I$ by applying the elementary row operation ${R}_{2}:=(-3){R}_{2},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :=(-3){R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

- The matrix $C$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from $I$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

Therefore, only $A$ and $B$ are elementary matrices.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Inverse of an Elementary 3x3 Matrix
questions.problem:
Find the inverse of the elementary matrix 
$E=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
We write down $E$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}[E\,|\,I\,] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{2}:=-\frac{1}{3}{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore, 

$$
{E}^{-1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Two Distinct Eigenvalues
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 2 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=3.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a $3\times 3$ matrix with the following eigenvalues:

- $\lambda =-2$ of algebraic multiplicity $2$

- $\lambda =3$ of algebraic multiplicity $1$

As a result, we have one $1\times 1$ Jordan block ${J}_{1}(3)$ corresponding to $\lambda =3.$
However, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =-2:$

- *Case I.* We may get the single $2\times 2$ Jordan block ${J}_{2}(-2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may get a composition of two $1\times 1$ Jordan blocks, namely ${J}_{1}(-2)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(-2).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we obtain in this situation, let's find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =-2.$

Computing $A+2I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-8 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 2 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}]+2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 4 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+2I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ -9 & 4 & -2 \\ 9 & 1 & 7\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{3}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ 0 & 10 & 10 \\ 0 & -5 & -5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 & -8 \\ 0 & 10 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A+2I)=1,$ there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2,$ say, ${v}_{1}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0
$$

Therefore, we have *case I*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{1}(3)\,⊕\,{J}_{2}(-2)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Jordan Canonical Form of a 3x3 Matrix With Only One Eigenvalue
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

The matrix above has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}={\lambda }_{2}={\lambda }_{3}=1.$ Find a Jordan canonical form of the matrix.
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that we are given a non-scalar $3\times 3$ matrix that has the eigenvalue $\lambda =1$ of algebraic multiplicity $3.$ 

As a result, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =1:$

- *Case I.* We may have the single $3\times 3$ Jordan block ${J}_{3}(1).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =1$ form the following chain:

$$
{v}_{3}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }{v}_{2}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may have a composition of one $2\times 2$ and one $1\times 1$ Jordan block, say ${J}_{2}(1)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(1).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =1$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we have in this situation, we find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =1.$

Computing $A-I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\text{nullity}(A-I)=1,$ there will be only one eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1,$ say, ${v}_{1}.$ So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{3}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }{v}_{2}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0
$$

 

Therefore, we have *case I*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{3}(1)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

 

**Note:** The Jordan canonical form is unique up to the order of the Jordan blocks.

questions.problem:
$$

As a result, there are two possibilities for the Jordan blocks corresponding to $\lambda =5:$

- *Case I.* We may have the single $3\times 3$ Jordan block ${J}_{3}(5).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =5$ form the following chain: 

$$
{v}_{3}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{2}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0
$$

- *Case II.* We may have a composition of one $2\times 2$ and one $1\times 1$ Jordan block, say ${J}_{2}(5)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(5).$ This happens when the generalized eigenvectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2}$ and ${v}_{3}$ corresponding to $\lambda =5$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

To figure out which of the cases we have in this situation, we find the number of linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to $\lambda =5.$

Computing $A-5I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 6 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we reduce this matrix to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the matrix above, there is one pivot column (the 2nd  one). So, the rank of $A-5I$ is $1.$ Using the rank-nullity theorem, we have that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{nullity}(A-5I) & =3-\text{rank}(A-5I) \\  & =3-1 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the generalized eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =1$ form the following chains:

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{2}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {v}_{3}\overset{A-5I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have *case II*, and $A$ has the following Jordan canonical form:

$$
{J}_{2}(5)\,⊕\,{J}_{1}(5)=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{J}_{2}(-2) & : & {v}_{2}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }{v}_{1}\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0 &  \\ {J}_{1}(1) & : & {v}_{3}\overset{A-I\,}{\to }0 & \end{aligned}

$$

Among the given vectors, only 
$z$
is an eigenvector of $A,$ since

$$

and we can write

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\overset{A+2I\,}{\to }0.\end{aligned}
$$

The other vectors do not satisfy this condition.

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Exponential Equation by Factoring
questions.problem: What is the product of solutions of the equation ${x}^{2}\cdot {7}^{2-x}-{7}^{2-x}=0?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we factor the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot {7}^{2-x}-{7}^{2-x} & =0 \\ ({x}^{2}-1)\cdot {7}^{2-x} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

We can now apply the zero product property, which states that $ab=0$ if and only if $a=0$ or $b=0.$ This gives us two equations,

$$
{x}^{2}-1=0\,\text{and}\,{7}^{2-x}=0.
$$

We now solve each of these equations separately.

- The equation ${x}^{2}-1=0$ can be factored as

$$
(x+1)(x-1)=0,
$$

which leads to the solutions $x=-1,1.$

- The equation ${7}^{2-x}=0$ has no solutions because ${7}^{2-x}$ is positive for every real number $x.$

Therefore, the original equation has the solutions $x=-1,1,$ and their product is $-1\cdot 1=-1.$
