questions.knowledge_point: Surface Areas of Surfaces Defined as Z=F(X,Y): Non-Rectangular Domains
questions.problem: Consider the portion of the surface $z=x{y}^{2}$ whose projection onto the $xy$-plane is bounded by $y={x}^{2},$ $x=1,$ and the $x$-axis. Find a repeated integral expression for the surface area of this surface.
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=f(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface area of $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

In this case, our surface is given by

$$
z=x{y}^{2},\,(x,y)\in D
$$

where the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14066535/assets/1419b067fe92945249655c5d29498aa4d3b0269d79ebd237fd9ed2a713b70b6a.png)

Now, since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{y}^{2})={y}^{2}, \\ \frac{∂z}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{y}^{2})=2xy,\end{aligned}
$$

the surface area is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{({y}^{2})}^{2}+(2xy)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}+4{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}\sqrt{1+{y}^{4}+4{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Flux Integral as a Surface Integral
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨{z}^{2},\,x,\,y-{z}^{2}⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,-1,\,2⟩\,.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S=\frac{1}{3}{∬}_{S}\boxed{}\,\text{d}S,
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨{z}^{2},\,x,\,y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,-1,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨{z}^{2},\,x,\,y-{z}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,-1,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2{z}^{2}-x+2(y-{z}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{2y-x}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{2y-x}{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{∬}_{S}2y-x\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing Flux Through a Surface as a Double Integral
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v),$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨3x,\,3y,\,z⟩,\,r(u,v)=⟨u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,{u}^{2}⟩,\,(u,v)\in D⊂{R}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,u⟩.$*
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Notice we are told that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,u⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨3x,\,3y,\,z⟩{|}_{x=u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\,y=u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\,z={u}^{2}} \\  & =⟨3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,{u}^{2}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,{u}^{2}⟩\cdot ⟨-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v,\,-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v,\,u⟩ \\  & =3u\operatorname{cos}⁡v\cdot (-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡v)+3u\operatorname{sin}⁡v\cdot (-2{u}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡v)+{u}^{2}\cdot u \\  & =-6{u}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡v+{sin}^{2}⁡v)+{u}^{3} \\  & =-5{u}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,-5{u}^{3}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Express Surface Integrals as Repeated Integrals
questions.problem:
Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}yz,$ where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=-x+y$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$
This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-x+y)=-1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-x+y)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(-1)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,{x}^{2}y(-x+y)\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\sqrt{3}(-{x}^{3}y+{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing Flux Over a Surface as a Repeated Integral
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x+y,\,2x-y,\,x+z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=2x-2y$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $-1\le y\le 2.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,2u-2v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D={(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,-1\le v\le 2}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-2⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\,2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨x+y,\,2x-y,\,x+z⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=2u-2v} \\  & =⟨u+v,\,2u-v,\,u+(2u-2v)⟩ \\  & =⟨u+v,\,2u-v,\,3u-2v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨u+v,\,2u-v,\,3u-2v⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,2,\,1⟩ \\  & =(u+v)\cdot (-2)+(2u-v)\cdot (2)+(3u-2v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-2u-2v+4u-2v+3u-2v \\  & =5u-6v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing Flux Over a Surface as a Repeated Integral
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined by $z=x-y$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Using the parametrization $x=u$ and $y=v,$ the flux of $F$ through $S$ can be expressed as

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,u-v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D={(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 1,\,0\le v\le 1}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,1⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(u-v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =⟨|\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,-|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}|,\,|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}|⟩ \\  & =⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=u-v} \\  & =⟨(u-v)v,\,(u-v)u,\,uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨(u-v)v,\,(u-v)u,\,uv⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =(u-v)v\cdot (-1)+(u-v)u\cdot (1)+uv\cdot 1 \\  & =-uv+{v}^{2}+{u}^{2}-uv+uv \\  & ={u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨zy,\,xz,\,xy⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}({u}^{2}-uv+{v}^{2})\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing Flux Through a Surface as a Double Integral
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v),$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨xz,\,y,\,xz⟩,\,r(u,v)=⟨u,\,uv,\,v⟩,\,(u,v)\in D⊂{R}^{2}.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}\boxed{}\,\text{d}A
$$

what is the missing expression?

*Hint: You can use the fact that ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨v,\,-1,\,u⟩.$*
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Notice we are told that the fundamental vector product for our surface is

$$
{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}=⟨v,\,-1,\,u⟩.
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨xz,\,y,\,xz⟩{|}_{x=u\,y=uv\,z=v} \\  & =⟨uv,\,uv,\,uv⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨uv,\,uv,\,uv⟩\cdot ⟨v,\,-1,\,u⟩ \\  & =uv\cdot v+uv\cdot (-1)+uv\cdot u \\  & =u{v}^{2}-uv+{u}^{2}v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,u{v}^{2}-uv+{u}^{2}v\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
For a surface $S$ given by $y=2x{z}^{3}$ for $(x,z)\in D,$ the flux of the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(\,{z}^{3}+Q-\,x{z}^{2})\,\text{d}A.
$$

From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?

*Hint: The orientation of $S$ should be chosen such that the unit normal vector has a positive  $j$-component.*
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $y=2x{z}^{3},$ it can be parameterized as

$$
r(x,z)=⟨x,\,2x{z}^{3},z⟩.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\,2{z}^{3},\,0⟩ \\ {r}_{z}^{′} & =⟨0,\,6x{z}^{2},\,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{z}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 2{z}^{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 6x{z}^{2} & 1\end{aligned}|=⟨2{z}^{3},\,-1,\,6x{z}^{2}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

However, notice that the $j$-component is negative. Therefore, we select the normal vector that points in the *opposite* direction:

$$
{r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{x}^{′}=-{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{z}^{′}=⟨-2{z}^{3},\,1,\,-6x{z}^{2}⟩
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,z))\cdot ({r}_{z}^{′}\times {r}_{x}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\,Q,R\,⟩\cdot ⟨-2{z}^{3},\,1,\,-6x{z}^{2}⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-2P\,{z}^{3}+Q-6R\,x{z}^{2}\,)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating Flux Over a Surface
questions.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral

$$
{∬}_{S}⟨\frac{1}{z},\,\frac{xy}{z},\,z⟩\cdot \text{d}S
$$

where the surface $S$ is defined by $z={e}^{x-y}$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le x.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}{e}^{x-y}={e}^{x-y} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}{e}^{x-y}=-{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨\frac{1}{z},\,\frac{xy}{z},\,z⟩{|}_{z={e}^{x-y}} \\  & =⟨{e}^{-(x-y)},\,xy{e}^{-(x-y)},\,{e}^{x-y}⟩ \\  & =⟨{{{e}^{y-x}}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{xy{e}^{y-x}}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{{e}^{x-y}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨\frac{1}{z},\,\frac{xy}{z},\,z⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-{e}^{y-x}\cdot {e}^{x-y}-(xy{e}^{y-x})\cdot (-{e}^{x-y})+{e}^{x-y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-1+xy+{e}^{x-y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{x}(-1+xy+{e}^{x-y})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[-y+\frac{x{y}^{2}}{2}-{e}^{x-y}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-x+\frac{{x}^{3}}{2}-1+{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{8}-x+{e}^{x}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(-\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{8}-1+e)-1 \\  & =-\frac{19}{8}+e\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Determining the Critical Points of a Transformation
questions.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}u+2w \\ v-u \\ uw\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)=u+2w,\,y(u,v,w)=v-u,\,z(u,v,w)=uw.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =2 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =1 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =w & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =u\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ w & 0 & u\end{aligned}| \\  & =1|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & u\end{aligned}|+2|\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ w & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =1(u-0)+2(0-w) \\  & =u-2w.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$

questions.problem:
Find the locations of all of the critical points of the transformation $T,$ where $T$ is defined as

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{u} \\ {e}^{u+w} \\ uv+w\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={e}^{u},\,y(u,v,w)={e}^{u+w},\,z(u,v,w)=uv+w.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & ={e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =0 \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & ={e}^{u+w} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & ={e}^{u+w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =v & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =u & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u} & 0 & 0 \\ {e}^{u+w} & 0 & {e}^{u+w} \\ v & u & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u}|\begin{aligned}0 & {e}^{u+w} \\ u & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u}(0-u{e}^{u+w}) \\  & =-u{e}^{2u+w}.\end{aligned}
$$

The function has critical points when $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)}=0.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ -u{e}^{2u+w} & =0 \\ u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The equation $u=0$ defines the plane $u=0,$ i.e., $vw$-plane.

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{u}^{2}-{w}^{2} \\ w{e}^{u} \\ u-v\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
For a transformation 

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v \\ w\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}x(u,v,w) \\ y(u,v,w) \\ z(u,v,w)\end{aligned}],
$$

the Jacobian determinant of $T,$ denoted $\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)},$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} & \frac{∂x}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v} & \frac{∂y}{∂w} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & \frac{∂z}{∂v} & \frac{∂z}{∂w}\end{aligned}|.\end{aligned}
$$

Here, we have 

$$
x(u,v,w)={u}^{2}-{w}^{2},\,y(u,v,w)=w{e}^{u},\,z(u,v,w)=u-v.
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & =2u & \,\frac{∂x}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂x}{∂w} & =-2w \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & =w{e}^{u} & \,\frac{∂y}{∂v} & =0 & \,\frac{∂y}{∂w} & ={e}^{u} \\ \frac{∂z}{∂u} & =1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂v} & =-1 & \,\frac{∂z}{∂w} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the corresponding Jacobian determinant is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =|\begin{aligned}2u & 0 & -2w \\ w{e}^{u} & 0 & {e}^{u} \\ 1 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u|\begin{aligned}0 & {e}^{u} \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}|-2w|\begin{aligned}w{e}^{u} & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2u(0+{e}^{u})-2w(-w{e}^{u}-0) \\  & =2u{e}^{u}+2{w}^{2}{e}^{u} \\  & =2{e}^{u}({w}^{2}+u).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y,z)}{∂(u,v,w)} & =0 \\ 2{e}^{u}({w}^{2}+u) & =0 \\ {w}^{2}+u & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14081085/assets/e61f3d7c23ef7876bec2f11c93974551058bcd32f28745898604926d84dbcfee.png)

Consider the vector field $F=⟨y,\,0,\,2x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that represents the boundary of the solid shown above. Let $D$ be the projection of the solid onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=0$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper plane ${S}_{1}.$ 

Since the positive orientation is upward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨y,0,2x⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider the lower cone ${S}_{2}.$

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-2)=\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=y,\,Q=0,\,R=2x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂h}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂h}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-y\cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-0\cdot \frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}+2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-2x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x\,\text{d}A+{∬}_{D}(\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{xy}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider a small rectangle $Δ$ whose bottom-left corner is located at the point $(-2,2)$ with sides parallel to the coordinate axes in the $uv$-plane and whose area is $\delta A.$ Which of the following gives the best approximation for the area of the image of this rectangle under the action of the transformation $T,$ given by

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} \\ {u}^{3}+v\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the absolute value of the Jacobian determinant gives the local area scale factor of the transformation at that point:

$$
\text{Area}(T(Δ))≈|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\cdot {{\text{Area}(Δ)}_{⏟}}_{\delta A}
$$

 

Computing the corresponding Jacobian determinant, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂u} & \frac{∂x}{∂v} \\ \frac{∂y}{∂u} & \frac{∂y}{∂v}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}{e}^{u+v} & {e}^{u+v} \\ 3{u}^{2} & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & ={e}^{u+v}\cdot 1-3{u}^{2}\cdot {e}^{u+v} \\  & ={e}^{u+v}(1-3{u}^{2}) \\ {\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|}_{(-2,2)} & ={e}^{u+v}(1-3{u}^{2})\,{|}_{u=-2\,v=2} \\  & ={e}^{-2+2}(1-3(-2)^{2}) \\  & =-11\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(T(Δ)) & ≈|-11|\cdot \delta A \\  & =11\,\delta A.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is

Consider the vector field $F=⟨-y,\,0,\,x⟩$ and the closed surface $S$ that encloses the finite region between the hemisphere $z=1-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ and the plane $z=1.$ Let $D$ be the projection of $S$ onto the $xy$-plane. The flux of $F$ across $S$ can be expressed in terms of a double integral as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∬}_{D}\,\,\text{d}A.
$$

Which of the following could be the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
Since we have a closed surface, the positive orientation is outward-pointing by convention. So,

- the upper surface ${S}_{1}:z=g(x,y)=1$ is oriented upward, and

- the lower surface ${S}_{2}:z=h(x,y)=1-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}$ is oriented downward.

Now, we write down the flux across each of the surfaces separately.

- Consider the upper plane ${S}_{1}.$

Since the positive orientation is upward, the unit normal vector to the plane is $n=⟨0,0,1⟩.$ As a result, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨-y,0,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,0,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

- Consider lower hemisphere ${S}_{2}.$ 

We compute the partial derivatives of $z=h(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=\frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}})=\frac{y}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote $F=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩,$ then

$$
P=-y,\,Q=0,\,R=x.
$$

 

As a result, since the positive orientation is downward, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S & =-{∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(-(-y)\cdot \frac{x}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-(0)\cdot \frac{y}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}(\frac{xy}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux across the entire surface is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S+{∬}_{{S}_{2}}F\cdot \text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{D}(\frac{xy}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x-\frac{xy}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}-x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{xy}{\sqrt{9-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}{∬}_{{S}_{1}}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot (-\frac{x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})-(0)\cdot (-\frac{y}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}})+(-x))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}-x)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Line Integral Using Stokes' Theorem
questions.problem:
Let $C$ be the intersection of the paraboloid $z=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes $x+y=1,$ $x=0,$ and $y=0.$ Given that the curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above and $\text{curl}\,F=⟨-2z,\,0,\,0⟩,$ the circulation of $F$ along $C$ can be written as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr=
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the paraboloid $z=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our paraboloid $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨-2z,\,0,\,0⟩{|}_{z=10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}} \\  & =⟨-2(10-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}),\,0,\,0⟩ \\  & =⟨{{2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-20}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{0}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-20)\cdot (-2x)-0\cdot (-2y)+0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(4{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-40x)\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071512/assets/c181e209cca01a1d6e372caa7f7810a5fa4aa9f177595bd92f937a7cba8b8a75.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(4{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-40x)\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1-x}\,4{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{2}-40x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Type of Image Formed by a Linear Transformation
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14073713/assets/e2ab6906100a96a123b4b1520613f1e38fe2c7e77af390a8efe0596a2861727d.png)

Consider the linear transformation $T$ with matrix representation $T,$ given by

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

What would be the image of the triangle shown above under the action of $T?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that for any linear transformation $T$ with associated $2\times 2$ matrix $T,$ we have one of the following three possibilities:

- If $T$ is non-singular, i.e., $det(T)\ne 0,$ then the image of a two-dimensional object is a two-dimensional object. In particular, the image of a polygon with $n$ vertices is a polygon with $n$ vertices.

- If $T$ is singular, i.e., $det(T)=0,$ we have two additional subcases:

- If $T$ has at least one nonzero entry, then the image of a two-dimensional object is a one-dimensional line segment.

- If $T$ is the zero matrix, then the image of a two-dimensional object is the point $(0,0),$ the origin of the coordinate system.

Since $T$ is the zero matrix, the image of our object under the action of $T$ is the origin.

questions.knowledge_point: Swapping the Order of Integration by Changing the Projection Type
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072974/assets/c420d45ca9418fd29889d91a49cce4ae80bb71bdfd4e4aa701b495cc8d87335f.png)

The triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over the region $R$ (shown above) can be expressed as the following repeated integral:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}+y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

Rewrite this repeated integral by integrating first with respect to $z,$ then $x,$ and then $y.$
questions.worked_solution:
From the given repeated integral, we see that $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2},\,\,0\le z\le {x}^{2}+y}
$$

We wish to rewrite our triple integral as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(y)}^{{v}_{2}(y)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,y)}^{{u}_{2}(x,y)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y
$$

Since both repeated integrals first integrate with respect to $z,$ the $z$-limits remain the same as before:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(y)}^{{v}_{2}(y)}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}+y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ of $R$ onto the $xy$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072974/assets/8b7cfa72ed3dbfb121039c6e64b843d83489878a9f457fb1386e455e7d9649ec.png)

The region $D$ is a type I region in the $xy$-plane:

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 1,\,\,0\le y\le {x}^{2}}
$$

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y,$ we write $D$ as a type II region.

Notice that the left boundary of the region, written in the form $x=x(y),$ is 

$$
y={x}^{2}\,⟹\,x=\sqrt{y}
$$

and the right boundary of the region is

$$
x=1.
$$

Then, the type II representation of the region $D$ is

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,\sqrt{y}\le x\le 1},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14072974/assets/f49af5da2e4f1f281700e16c4659fabfcd0b15661947ca985d38f208f8563877.png)

Therefore, by swapping the order of integration, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{\sqrt{y}}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{x}^{2}+y}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Maclaurin Expansion of a Sum of Functions Using Standard Maclaurin Expansions
questions.problem: Find the first four non-zero terms of the Maclaurin expansion of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Maclaurin expansion of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) & =x-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}+\frac{{x}^{5}}{5!}-⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

Replacing $x$ with $2x$ we get

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{4!}-⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the expansions for $\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)$ and $\operatorname{cos}⁡(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & =(2x-\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{4{x}^{5}}{15}-⋯)+(1-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}+\frac{{x}^{4}}{4!}-⋯) \\  & =1+2x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}-\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Line Integral Using Stokes' Theorem
questions.problem:
Let $C$ be the intersection of the surface $z=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ and the boundary of the infinite vertical column enclosed by the planes $x=\pm 1,$ and $y=\pm 1.$ Given that the curve $C$ is oriented counter-clockwise when viewed from above and $\text{curl}\,F=⟨x,\,y,\,-2z⟩,$ the circulation of $F$ along $C$ can be written as 

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr=
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $S$ be an oriented piecewise-smooth surface bounded by a simple, closed, piecewise-smooth boundary $C$ with positive orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $S,$ then Stokes' theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S.
$$

There are many surfaces whose boundary is the curve $C$ representing the intersection of the surface $z=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}$ and the boundary of our infinite vertical column. One such surface is our surface $S$ with the equation 

$$
z=g(x,y)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}} \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})=\frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into expression for $\text{curl}\,F:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{curl}\,F\,{|}_{z=g(x,y)} & =⟨x,\,y,\,-2z⟩{|}_{z=1/({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)} \\  & =⟨{{x}_{⏟}}_{P},\,{{y}_{⏟}}_{Q},\,{{-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1}}_{⏟}}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\text{curl}\,F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-x\cdot \frac{-2x}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-y\cdot \frac{-2y}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}-\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is region enclosed by the projection of $C$ onto the $xy$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14071512/assets/b215ec1e3330f96e7e606e085721b2dd1f50d113f0151e36ec98e6d0a6f54e73.png)

Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}\,-\frac{2}{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)^{2}}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Curvature of a Plane Curve Given in Parametric Form
questions.problem:
The curvature of the plane curve $r(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+t\,j$ is given by 

$$
κ(t)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{},\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

 
What is the missing part of the expression?
questions.worked_solution:
The curvature $κ(t)$ of a plane curve $r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j$ is given by

$$
κ(t)=\frac{|{x}^{′}(t){y}^{″}(t)-{y}^{′}(t){x}^{″}(t)|}{([{x}^{′}(t)]^{2}+[{y}^{′}(t)]^{2})^{3/2}}.
$$

Along our curve, we have

$$
x(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,y(t)=t.
$$

First, we calculate the derivatives of the components:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t,\, & {y}^{′}(t) & =1 \\ {x}^{″}(t) & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\, & {y}^{″}(t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting these into the formula for the curvature, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}κ(t) & =\frac{|(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 0-(-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\cdot 1|}{{((\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+{1}^{2})}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{|\operatorname{cos}⁡t|}{{({sin}^{2}⁡t+1)}^{3/2}} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\sqrt{{({sin}^{2}⁡t+1)}^{3}}}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that we removed the absolute value because cosine is positive for $t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].$

{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{2}}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{2}}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{2}f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx.
$$

so that it is integrated first with respect to $y,$ then $z,$ then $x.$

We wish to find limits of integration ${u}_{1}(x,z),$ ${u}_{2}(x,z),$ ${v}_{1}(x),$ ${v}_{2}(x),$ $a,$ and $b$ such that

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{2}}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{2}}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{2}f(x,y,z)\,dz\,dy\,dx={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{{v}_{1}(x)}^{{v}_{2}(x)}{\int }_{{u}_{1}(x,z)}^{{u}_{2}(x,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x.
$$

From the repeated integral, we see that the region of integration $R$ can be written as a type I region as follows:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le x\le \sqrt[3]{2},\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{2},\,\,{y}^{3}\le z\le 2}
$$

Now, let's sketch the region. Since it is a type I region, we first sketch the projection onto the $xy$-plane, given by

$$
E={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le \sqrt[3]{2},\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{2}}.
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/58a9056015b3dad91ec7ae64bff893c8c6c2cce6480c979545e423cbe105ef03.png)

Then, the region $R$ is shown in the diagram below, where ${y}^{3}\le z\le 2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/2fdd6a15b4ddadfc3ee24af5e35e2a87e9e963ceeefbf858b704d78ee0b78513.png)

To change the order of integration from $\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x$ to $\text{d}y\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}x,$ we write $R$ as a type III region and its projection $D$ onto the $xz$-plane as a type I *plane* region.

To visualize this, imagine firing an arrow through the region parallel to the $y$-axis and in the direction of increasing $y,$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/65da730d32f200b8f9da004ee8cf6b7e79095e323961f4a5b6dfa0bddeace42b.png)

The arrow enters the region through the left boundary and leaves through the right boundary:

- The right boundary of the region, written in the form $y=(x,z),$ is

$$
z={y}^{3}\,⟹\,y=\sqrt[3]{z}
$$

- The left boundary of the region is

$$
y=0.
$$

Therefore, the type III representation of $R$ is

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(x,z)\in D,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{z}},
$$

as shown in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/1743f540a85fc1c266c84da8f34b2012516b7bbc98d113cf7c62ba3bba8173c1.png)

We now consider the projection $D$ as a type II plane region in the $xz$-plane with the top curve given by

$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14073682/assets/b76bf84e1179bec6a1e8e357c6cc628eee95c1663e6f0ff375135612a6f275de.png)

questions.knowledge_point: Writing the Flux Across a Closed Surface as a Triple Integral
questions.problem:
Let $S$ be the boundary of the rectangular prism enclosed by the planes $x=-1,$ $x=0,$ $y=1,$ $y=2,$ $z=0,$ $z=1.$ Given that the surface $S$ is positively (outward) oriented and $F=xy\,i+2y\,j+{x}^{2}zk,$ the flux of $F$ across $S$ can be written as 

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.
$$

What is the missing part of the expression?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $R$ be a simple solid region bounded by a closed surface $S$ with positive (outward) orientation. If a vector field $F$ has continuous partial derivatives for all its components in an open region in space that contains $R,$ then the divergence theorem states that

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS={∭}_{R}\text{div}\,F\,\text{d}V.
$$

Computing the divergence of $F,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)+\frac{∂}{∂y}(2y)+\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}z) \\  & =y+2+{x}^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}+y+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R$ be the solid region enclosed by $S.$ Then, using the divergence theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot dS & ={∭}_{R}({x}^{2}+y+2)\,\text{d}V \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,{x}^{2}+y+2\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Identifying the Local Extrema of a Multivariable Function
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14070363/assets/b698fe735caaf3bc260c1e921bb95596df8869eba67ec9ce72484b4d86cc8c69.png)

The graph of the function $z=f(x,y)$ is shown above. Which of the points shown are local minimum points?
questions.worked_solution:
A function $f(x,y)$ has a local minimum point at $(a,b)$ if $f(x,y)\ge f(a,b)$ for all points $(x,y)$ in a neighborhood of $(a,b).$ 

In other words, we can take a neighborhood of $(x,y)$-values such that the point $(x,y,f(x,y))$ is the lowest point on the graph in the neighborhood.

Such regions exist for the points $A$ and $D.$ Hence $A$ and $D$ are local minimum points.

**Note**: For the point $D({x}_{D},{y}_{D},{z}_{D}),$ there are points $(x,y)$ in the surrounding regions such that $f({x}_{D},{y}_{D})=f(x,y).$ However, since the definition of local extrema is non-strict, $f(x,y)\ge f(a,b)$, the point $D$ does satisfy the conditions for a local minimum.

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Derivative of a Vector Function
questions.problem:
For the transformation $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2},$ defined as

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}2xy \\ {e}^{xy}\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}],
$$

calculate ${f}^{′}(x).$
questions.worked_solution:
Suppose a transformation $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ is defined by 

$$
f:[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}{f}_{1}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ {f}_{2}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}) \\ ⋮ \\ {f}_{m}({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n})\end{aligned}],
$$

 

where ${f}_{1},{f}_{2},…,{f}_{m}$ are scalar functions with $n$ variables. If $f$ is differentiable at $x,$ then the total derivative of $f$ at $x,$ denoted ${f}^{′}(x),$ is given by the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have the following:

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2xy)=2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2xy)=2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy})=y{e}^{xy},\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy})=x{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2y & 2x \\ y{e}^{xy} & x{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Moment of Inertia About a Perpendicular Axis Using Polar Coordinates
questions.problem:
A circular plate of mass $2\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region of a disk $D$ of radius $2\,\text{m}$ centered at the origin.
Find the moment of inertia of the plate about a line perpendicular to $D$ at a distance of $4\,\text{m}$ from a parallel line passing through its center of mass.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, notice that the region $D$ can be expressed in polar coordinates as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

The area of the circular plate $D$ is $A=\pi \cdot {2}^{2}=4\pi \,{\text{m}}^{2}.$
Since the plate has a uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{2}{4\pi }=\frac{1}{2\pi }\,\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},
$$

and its center of mass is its centroid $(0,0).$

Then, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Maximum Speed of a Particle
questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $(4-x)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $P$ has velocity $v=6\,m/s$ at the origin, find the maximum velocity of the particle.
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14070857/assets/d4e5b78932f8ff6155ac81e12538eb31ac211c9d27d6a2b0c67542527ccd3b2a.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(4-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4-x.
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first or second derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}4-x & =0 \\ x & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=4\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,4)$ | $4$ | $(4,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $2$ |  | $6$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $2>0$ | $0$ | $-2<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=4\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=4-x.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int (4-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=4x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=6\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(6)^{2} & =4(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2}+C \\ C & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =4x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}+18 \\ {v}^{2} & =8x-{x}^{2}+36 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-{x}^{2}+8x+36}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-{x}^{2}+8x+36}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(4)=\sqrt{-(4)^{2}+8(4)+36}=2\sqrt{13}\,m/s
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Second Derivative of a Function Given Its First Derivative
questions.problem:
Find ${f}^{″}(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})$ for the function $f(x,y)$ given that
${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}10xy & 5{x}^{2}-2y\end{aligned}]$
questions.worked_solution:
For a function $f:{R}^{n}\to R,$ given by

$$
f:{{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ ⋮ \\ {x}_{n}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{x}⟶f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}),
$$

the second derivative of $f$ is given by the $n\times n$ matrix

$$
{f}^{″}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{1}∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}^{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{2}∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋮ \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}_{n}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{f}^{″}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}].
$$

First, notice that since ${f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}10xy & 5{x}^{2}-2y\end{aligned}],$ 
 we must have

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂x}=10xy,\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=5{x}^{2}-2y.
$$

Now, we compute the second partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(10xy)=10y\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(5{x}^{2}-2y)=10x \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(10xy)=10x\, & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(5{x}^{2}-2y)=-2\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x,y) & =[\begin{aligned}10y & 10x \\ 10x & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate this matrix at $(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}).$ This gives

$$
{f}^{″}(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})=[\begin{aligned}5 & 5 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Applying the Work-Energy Principle To Find the Work Done by a Force
questions.problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's acceleration is $(4t+1)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=3\,m/s$ when $t=0\,s,$ calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
questions.worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The acceleration of the particle is given by $a(t)=4t+1,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (4t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{t}^{2}+t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
3=2(0)^{2}+0+C\,⟹\,C=3.
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2{t}^{2}+t+3.$
In particular, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1$, is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=2(1)^{2}+1+3=6\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)=2(2)^{2}+2+3=13\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {13}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {6}^{2} \\  & =338-72 \\  & =266\,J.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & ={\int }_{{x}_{1}}^{{x}_{2}}F(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(3{x}^{2}+2)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{3}+2x]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =8+4-0 \\  & =12\,J\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {7}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 1\cdot {v}_{0}^{2} \\ 12 & =\frac{49}{2}-\frac{1}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}_{0}^{2} & =\frac{25}{2} \\ {v}_{0}^{2} & =25 \\ {v}_{0} & =\pm 5.\end{aligned}

Two point masses $A$ and $B$ are connected by a rigid, massless rod of length $10\,m$ that is perfectly balanced on a fulcrum, as shown above. If $B$ has mass $3\,kg$ and is $4\,m$ from the fulcrum, find the mass of $A.$

Let $m$ be the mass of $A.$
The length of the rod is $10\,m$ and the distance between the fulcrum and $B$ is $4\,m.$ So, the distance between the fulcrum and $A$ is

$$
10-4=6\,m,
$$

Let's write down the moment of each mass about the fulcrum:

- The moment of mass $A$ equals $-m\cdot 6=-6m\,\text{kg}\cdot \text{m}$ (negative since the motion induced by this mass would be counterclockwise).

- The moment of mass $B$ equals $3\cdot 4=12\,\text{kg}\cdot \text{m}$ (positive since the motion induced by this mass would be clockwise).

The *principle of moments* tells us that for the two masses to balance perfectly, the sum of the moments must equal zero.

Therefore, in this case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}12-6m & =0 \\ 6m & =12 \\ m & =2\,kg.\end{aligned}
$$

The graph $z=f(x,y)$ is shown above. What are the global maximum points of the function?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we recall the following definitions:

- The global maximum of a function is the largest value it attains on its domain. There can only be (at most) one global maximum.

- A global maximum point is a point $(x,y,z)$ where a function reaches a global maximum. There can be zero, one, or many global maximum points.

For our function, the maximum value reached by the function is $f(x,y)=3.$ Therefore, the global maximum is $3.$ The function reaches this value when $(x,y)=(-2,1),$ so the global maximum point is $(-2,1,3).$

questions.knowledge_point: Writing First-Order Linear ODEs in Standard Form
questions.problem:
Write the following first-order linear ODE in standard form.

$$
2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=1-4y\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Converting the given equation to standard form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =1-4y\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =1+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}_{⏟}}_{P(x)}y & ={{\frac{1+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}_{⏟}}_{Q(x)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $Q(x)=\frac{1+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Distance Between Two Parallel Axes
questions.problem:
A circular plate of mass $3\,\text{kg}$ with uniform mass density occupies the region of a disk $D$ of radius $2\,\text{m}$ and is centered at the origin.
Given that the moment of inertia of the plate about a line $l$ perpendicular to the plate is $15\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2},$ find the distance of the line $l$ from the center of mass of $D.$
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, notice that the region $D$ can be expressed in polar coordinates as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

The area of the circular plate $D$ is $A=\pi \cdot {2}^{2}=4\pi \,{\text{m}}^{2}.$
Since the plate has a uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{3}{4\pi }\,\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},
$$

and its center of mass is its centroid $(0,0).$

Then, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{4\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{3}{4\pi }\cdot \frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{2}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\frac{3}{4\pi }\cdot 4\cdot 2\pi  \\  & =6\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem and solving for $d,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\ 15 & =6+3{d}^{2} \\ 3{d}^{2} & =9 \\ {d}^{2} & =3 \\ d & =\sqrt{3}\,\text{m}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Moment of Inertia of a Rectangular Plate About a Perpendicular Axis
questions.problem:
A rectangular plate of mass $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{kg}$ and uniform mass density occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le 2},$
where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters.
Find the moment of inertia of the plate about a line perpendicular to $D$ at a distance of $\sqrt{6}\,\text{m}$ from a parallel line passing through its center of mass.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

The area of the rectangular plate $D$ is $A=2\cdot 2=4\,{\text{m}}^{2}.$
Since the plate has a uniform density, the mass density function is given by

$$
\lambda (x,y)=\frac{M}{A}=\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{4}=\frac{3}{8}\,\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},
$$

and its center of mass is its centroid:

$$
(\overset{¯}{x},\overset{¯}{y})=(\frac{-1+1}{2},\frac{0+2}{2})=(0,1)
$$

Then, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}((x-\overset{¯}{x})^{2}+(y-\overset{¯}{y})^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}3{x}^{2}+3(y-1)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{[3{x}^{2}y+(y-1)^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{-1}^{1}6{x}^{2}+2\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{[2{x}^{3}+2x]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}(2+2-(-2-2)) \\  & =1\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a line $\sqrt{6}\,\text{m}$ from the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\  & =1+{(\sqrt{6})}^{2}\cdot \frac{3}{2} \\  & =1+9 \\  & =10\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Moment of Inertia of a Rectangular Plate About a Perpendicular Axis
questions.problem:
A rectangular plate occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 3,\,0\le y\le 2}$
and has mass density function $\lambda (x,y)=2x,$ where $x$ and $y$ are measured in meters.
Given that the center of mass is at $(2,1),$ find the moment of inertia about a line perpendicular to $D$ at a distance of $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\,\text{m}$ from a parallel line passing through its center of mass.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, we find the mass of the plate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}2x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}2x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={x}^{2}{|}_{0}^{3}\cdot y{|}_{0}^{2} \\  & =9\cdot 2 \\  & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Next, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass $(2,1)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}((x-\overset{¯}{x})^{2}+(y-\overset{¯}{y})^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}((x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}((x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2})2x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}2x(x-2)^{2}+2x(y-1)^{2}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{[2x(x-2)^{2}y+\frac{2}{3}x(y-1)^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}4x(x-2)^{2}+\frac{4}{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{3}-16{x}^{2}+16x+\frac{4}{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{3}-16{x}^{2}+\frac{52}{3}x\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[{x}^{4}-\frac{16}{3}{x}^{3}+\frac{26}{3}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =81-144+78-0 \\  & =15\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a line $\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3}\,\text{m}$ from the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\  & =15+{(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3})}^{2}\cdot 18 \\  & =15+4 \\  & =19\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
A function $f(x,y)$ has a local maximum point at $(a,b)$ if $f(x,y)\le f(a,b)$ for all points $(x,y)$ in a neighborhood of $(a,b).$ 

In other words, we can take a neighborhood of $(x,y)$-values such that the point $(x,y,f(x,y))$ is the highest point on the graph in the neighborhood.

Such neighborhoods exist for the points $C$ and $D.$ Hence $C$ and $D$ are local maxima.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating Intercepts of Spheres and Ellipsoids
questions.problem: Given the ellipsoid $\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(y+2)^{2}}{8}+\frac{(z-1)^{2}}{4}=1$, find its intercepts with the $x$-axis.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the $x$-intercepts, we plug $y=0$ and $z=0$ into the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{16}+\frac{(0+2)^{2}}{8}+\frac{(0-1)^{2}}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{16}+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4} & =1 \\ \frac{(x-2)^{2}}{16} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ (x-2)^{2} & =4 \\ x-2 & =\pm 2 \\ x & =2\pm 2\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, we get the solutions $x=0$ and $x=4.$

Therefore, the intercepts with the $x$-axis are $(0,0,0)$ and $(4,0,0).$

questions.problem: Given the sphere $(x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}+(z-2)^{2}=9,$ what is the domain of $z=z(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
From the equation of the sphere, we make $z$ the subject as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}+(z-2)^{2} & =9 \\ (z-2)^{2} & =9-((x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}) \\ z-2 & =\pm \sqrt{9-((x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2})} \\ z & =2\pm \sqrt{9-((x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2})}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}9-((x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2})\ge 0 \\ (x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}\le 9\end{aligned}
$$

This inequality describes the interior and boundary of the circle 

$$
(x-3)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=9
$$

which is a circle of radius $3$ centered at $(3,1)$ in the $xy$-plane.

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Moment of Inertia About a Perpendicular Axis Using Polar Coordinates
questions.problem: Calculate the moment of inertia of a circular plate that occupies the region of an annulus $D$ centered at $O$ with inner radius $1\,\text{m},$ outer radius $\sqrt{2}\,\text{m},$ and mass density $\lambda (x,y)=\frac{|xy|}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},$ measured in $\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},$ about a line perpendicular to the ring passing through a point $3\,\text{m}$ from its center.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina of mass $M$ and a line ${l}_{M}$ perpendicular to the lamina passing through its center of mass, the parallel axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of the lamina about a line $l$ parallel to ${l}_{M}$ is given by

$$
{I}_{l}={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M,
$$

where $d$ is the distance between the lines, and ${I}_{M}$ and ${I}_{l}$ are the moments of inertia about the lines ${l}_{M}$ and $l,$ respectively.

First, notice that the region $D$ can be expressed in polar coordinates as

$$
D={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le \sqrt{2},\,\,0\le \theta <2\pi }.
$$

Since the mass density is symmetric in $x$ and $y,$ the center of mass is at $(0,0).$ The mass density function, in polar coordinates, is given by 

$$
\lambda (r,\theta )=\frac{|r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta |}{{r}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )|.
$$

Next, we find the mass of the plate as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2}|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )|\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}r\,\text{d}r\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )|\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2-1)\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =1\,\text{kg}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, the moment of inertia about the perpendicular line through the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{M} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}\frac{1}{2}|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )|\cdot {r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{2}|\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )|\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{r}^{4}{|}_{1}^{\sqrt{2}}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(4-1)\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta )]_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}\cdot (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{3}{2}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, applying the parallel axis theorem, the moment of inertia about a line $3\,\text{m}$ from the center of mass is

$$
\begin{aligned}I & ={I}_{M}+{d}^{2}M \\  & =\frac{3}{2}+{3}^{2}\cdot 1 \\  & =\frac{3}{2}+9 \\  & =\frac{21}{2}\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

The full expression describing all points on our hyperbolic cylinder is

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}-\frac{(y+1)^{2}}{4}=1,\,z=k
$$

where $k\in R$ can vary arbitrarily. 

The domain of any cylinder in the $xy$-plane is its base curve. Hence, in this case, the domain is

$$

Remember that the general equation of an ellipse centered at $(h,k)$ with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

In the given equation, we have $h=-1$ and $k=-3,$ so the center is located at $(-1,-3).$

In the given equation, we also have ${a}^{2}=5$ and ${b}^{2}=20.$

- Since ${a}^{2}=5,$ the length of the horizontal radius must be $a=\sqrt{5}.$

- Since ${b}^{2}=20,$ the length of the vertical radius must be $b=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5}.$

So the semi-major axis has length $b=2\sqrt{5},$ and the semi-minor axis has length $a=\sqrt{5}.$

Therefore, the major axis has length $2b=2\cdot 2\sqrt{5}=4\sqrt{5},$ and the minor axis has length $2a=2\cdot \sqrt{5}=2\sqrt{5}.$

$$

Therefore, the ellipse intercepts the $x$-axis at the points $(3-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3},0)$ and $(3+\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{3},0).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Global Maxima and Minima of a Function Whose Domain Is a Smooth Curve
questions.problem: Find the global extrema of the function $f(x,y)=1-{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$ on the closed region $D={(x,y)\,:\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 16}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $f(x,y)$ is continuous on the closed, bounded region $D,$ the function attains a global maximum and minimum on $D.$

To find the extreme values, we follow three steps.

**Step 1.** Find the critical points of $f$ inside the region. 

To determine the critical points, we solve ${f}^{′}=0.$ Computing the derivative gives

$$
{f}^{′}(x,y)=[\begin{aligned}-2x,\,2y\end{aligned}].
$$

The derivative exists at each point inside $D,$ and it equals zero when

$$
\begin{aligned}{\begin{aligned}-2x=0 \\ 2y=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,{\begin{aligned}x=0 \\ y=0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

This gives us a single point $(0,0)\in D,$ which we include in the list of candidates for the extrema.

**Step 2.**  Find the points on the boundary of $D$ that could give rise to extreme values. 

To find the boundary points that could give rise to extreme values, we parametrize the bounding circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$ This gives

$$
r=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,t\in [0,2\pi ).
$$

The values of $f$ on the boundary are given by the function

$$
\begin{aligned}F(t) & =f(x(t),y(t)) \\  & =f(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =1-(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =1-16{cos}^{2}⁡t+16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =1-16\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the critical points of $F(t)$ on the open interval $t\in (0,2\pi ),$ we solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(t) & =0 \\ (1-16\operatorname{cos}⁡2t)^{′} & =0 \\ 32\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation gives four solutions, namely

$$
t=\frac{\pi }{2},\,\pi ,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\in (0,2\pi ).
$$

We also have to check the endpoint of the interval $t=0.$ Therefore, the only values of $t$ that can give rise to extreme values are 

$$
t=0,\,\frac{\pi }{2},\,\pi ,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Evaluating the corresponding values of $x$ and $y$ on the boundary, we obtain four candidate points:

$$
(4,0),\,(0,4),\,(-4,0),\,(0,-4)
$$

**Step 3.** Evaluate $f(x,y)$ at each of the candidate points, and compare their values. 

Evaluating $f(x,y)$ at each of the points mentioned above, we get the following: 

| $(x,y)$ | $(0,0)$ | $(4,0)$ | $(0,4)$ | $(-4,0)$ | $(0,-4)$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x,y)$ | $1$ | $-15$ | $17$ | $-15$ | $17$ |

Therefore, on the closed region $D,$ we have that 

- $f$ attains the global minimum of $-15$ at the points $(4,0)$ and $(-4,0),$ and

- $f$ attains the global maximum of $17$ at the points $(0,4)$ and $(0,-4).$

Let $A$ be a $2\times 2$ matrix with eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-2$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=3$ corresponding to the eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ respectively, where

$$

$$

Given that the position of a particle at time $t$ seconds is given by the vector $x(t),$ and that $x(t)$ is the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),\,x(0)=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

find the position of the particle at $t=2$ seconds.
questions.worked_solution:
Given a system of first-order linear ODEs in the form

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),
$$

where $A$ has two distinct eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1},{\lambda }_{2}$ with corresponding eigenvectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2},$ the formula for the general solution is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our matrix differential equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & ={c}_{1}{v}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}+{c}_{2}{v}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t} \\  & ={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t},\,{c}_{1},{c}_{2}\in R.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the values of ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$, we substitute $t=0$ into the general solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(0) & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2(0)}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3(0)} & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ {c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}+{c}_{2} \\ 5{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}-{c}_{1}+{c}_{2}=3 \\ 5{c}_{1}-{c}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the equations, we get

$$
4{c}_{1}=4\,⟹\,{c}_{1}=1.
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-1+{c}_{2}=3\,⟹\,{c}_{2}=4.
$$

 

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
\begin{aligned}x(t) & =1[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+4[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate $x(2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}x(2) & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2(2)}+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{3(2)} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 5\end{aligned}]{e}^{-4}+[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]{e}^{6} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-{e}^{-4}+4{e}^{6} \\ 5{e}^{-4}-4{e}^{6}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-1.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The  maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$  

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving a First-Order ODE Using a Substitution
questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{y+2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{x}
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{-1}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-1}\,⟹\,y={z}^{-1}\,
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{z}^{-1}+2{x}^{2}{z}^{-2}}{x} \\ -\frac{1}{{z}^{2}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{xz}+\frac{2x}{{z}^{2}} \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{z}{x}-2x\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-\frac{z}{x}-2x \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z & =-2x\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,Q(x)=-2x\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}x\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}z) & =x\cdot (-2x) \\ x\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z & =-2{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz) & =-2{x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(xz)\,\text{d}x & =-\int 2{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ xz & =-\frac{2}{3}{x}^{3}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-2{x}^{3}}{3x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1} & =\frac{C-2{x}^{3}}{3x} \\ y & =\frac{3x}{C-2{x}^{3}}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

under the condition that $x>0.$

$$

where $C=3{C}_{1}.$

Now, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$

questions.problem: How many different ways can a group of four be made from a room of eighty people?

In general, the number of combinations of $n$ objects taken $r$ at a time is given by the formula

$$

$$

$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Where the Extrema of a Quadratic Form Is Attained Over an Ellipse
questions.problem: The maximum value of $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}+8{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+8{x}_{2}^{2},$ when ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2}=4,$ is $12.$ Find a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}]
$$

 Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

 

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1
$$

 This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=1$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}={x}_{2},$

 the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

 So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],
$$

 

 we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

 

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

 As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 8 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 8 \\ 8 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

 Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $||y||=1,$ as usual.

 Since we are told that the maximum value of the quadratic form is $12,$ we have

 

$$
max{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{max}=12.
$$

 Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=12:$

 

$$
\begin{aligned}B-12I & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 8 \\ 8 & 8\end{aligned}]-12[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-16 & 8 \\ 8 & -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-12I)y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

 

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

 Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{max}} & =P{u}_{\text{max}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
